new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE:, p.3, heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': 'Stress is penultimate unless that syllable peak is /ɨ/, in which case stress moves leftward until it reaches a vowel other than /ɨ/.' Confirmed verbatim from my own 150-dpi render of p.3 (the PDF text drops the barred-i glyph, printing '/ /'; the render shows /ɨ/ both times). Nothing else on tone or length; the bolded syllables in the following 'Syllable Patterns' table mark the exemplified syllable type in initial/medial/final position (OPD template), not stress, so they are not stress data. On the identity of the variety: OPD header 'Tainae (Ivori) Language [AGO], Kotidanga - Gulf Province, Trans New Guinea Phylum; Angan Stoc…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the penultimate syllable; if the penult's nucleus is the high central vowel /ɨ/, stress retracts leftward to the nearest syllable whose vowel is not /ɨ/ (i.e. penultimate with /ɨ/-avoidance, a quality-sensitive retraction).
new_statements.exceptions: Only the /ɨ/-avoidance clause. The OPD gives no exceptions list. Note: the stress-marked phonetic forms in Carlson 1991 Grammar Essentials sec. 1.4 mostly show penultimate stress ([fand'ewo], [afij'awo], [pufw'æri], [iwam'eri]) but a few trisyllables are marked with initial stress where the penult is not /ɨ/ (['animo] 'mosquito', [h'amdiro] 'snake', [n'agubwɪ] 'river (goal)'), so the OPD rule is a generalisation that the 1991 transcriptions do not follow without residue.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word (OPD suprasegmentals section; examples are citation forms). No tone or contrastive length reported; the section heading 'tone, stress, length' is the OPD template and only stress is filled
new_statements.identity_note: Both Carlson sources describe Tainae (also called Ivori), Kotidanga, Gulf Province, villages Piu, Kamanakwawa, Paingoni = Glottolog tain1253 / ISO ago; Grammar Essentials says data come from speakers 'representative of the various dialects within the language', no single dialect singled out.

tone_statements.quote: Tone and stress are combined in a complex unit which usually occurs in connection with the grammatical stem. Angaataha, with four tonemes, is noticeably different from the other Angan languages. In Angaataha stress is also linked to high tone. Thus Angaataha is like a 'tone language' and the others are more 'intonation languages'.

Family-wide 'Common Phonological Features' (sec. 2.152, pp.86-87; tone paragraph on p.87 = p.57): 'Tone and stress are combined in a complex unit' tied to the grammatical stem; only Angaataha (four tonemes, stress linked to high tone) is 'like a tone language', the other Angan languages (Ivori among them by implication) are 'more intonation languages'.
